articles.title: BioWare May Be Dead, But a Modder Has Rebuilt Mass Effect 3's Multiplayer Into the Legendary Edition
articles.summary: When the Mass Effect Legendary Edition came out in 2021, it included the single player campaign of all three original games, along with all the DLC. But while all the story content you could ever want was included, Mass Effect 3's multiplayer mode was conspicuously absent, despite having a dedicated fanbase.
articles.body:
When the Mass Effect Legendary Edition came out in 2021, it included the single player campaign of all three original games, along with all the DLC. But while all the story content you could ever want was included, Mass Effect 3's multiplayer mode was conspicuously absent, despite having a dedicated fanbase.

Now, just a few weeks after EA's shutdown of BioWare , a team of modders has successfully ported Mass Effect 3 's multiplayer to the Legendary Edition, with all the graphics and engine improvements that came with that re-release. The mod will be coming out on N7 Day – November 7th – and will be free to play, as long as you already own Mass Effect Legendary Edition.

I also got a chance to sit down with Mgamerz, who runs the ME3Tweaks team that created the mod, to talk about Mass Effect 3, and about the state of modding in 2026. And if you want to download the mod yourself, it's available now on Nexus Mods.

IGN: So, tell me a little bit about the project, and how you got started on basically porting the Mass Effect 3 multiplayer over to the Legendary Edition.

Mgamerz: Yeah, so my dev team, ME3Tweaks, and I run it. We ported Pinnacle Station back in 2021. Crazy effort. I don't know how we got that done in a two-month timeframe. And then we were doing other projects for two years, and then near the end of me working on LE2 Randomizer, which is a randomizer for legendary Mass Effect 2, someone discovered a copy of the Citadel in Mass Effect 2.

There's an area from the wards. I can't remember which game it was, but they found an area of the game that nobody knew about before, and you could load into and you're like, 'Well, this was clearly supposed to be something, and then they just never finished it.' It was a very early prototype. And it was like, 'Man, what if we could port something like that into another level?' And so I made this project called Project Wardle, Ward being the first part of it. (We have a bunch of stupid internal code names.)

And I eventually made it so we could port a Mass Effect 2 level into Mass Effect 3, and we fixed up the cover, because cover is just an unbelievable nightmare. It's very important for enemies to be able to use it. Gameplay's a huge component of why Mass Effect 3 is fun. And we got that working and then I was like, 'Well, man, what if we could port the multiplayer levels?' Because we did it for Pinnacle Station. We ported the old game. But Pinnacle Station is mostly just reused assets from Mass Effect 1.

Like 90% of it was just existing assets that they just reused. But multiplayer was totally different. It's like, yeah, none of this content exists. So the scope of work is just huge. So at the end of 2023, right as we finished LE2 Randomizer, literally on N7 day, I spun up a new Discord.

I invited a couple people and they're like, 'What's this Discord about?' I'm like, 'We're going to do something stupid. We're going to port [Mass Effect 3] Multiplayer.' And those were the first two messages I ever sent. I have some screenshots of it.

And then people were like, 'Yeah, you're joking, right?' And I'm like, 'No.' And then the last three years we've been working on it. It hasn't been constant. Last year I broke my arm, which set us back six to eight months.

But for the first two years, it was tons of prototyping. Within the first month of this project, we actually had multiplayer working. It was a proof of concept. And then we spent the next two years getting audio to port, from a different version of the audio engine because they upgraded it. It's like we got shaders building, which was a total nightmare because BioWare compiled the game with a bunch of sources that don't ship with the game.

And so we had to figure out 'how do we replicate that?' So that took a long time. And then it's like textures. We have a bunch more people that know how to do texture upscaling. The first two years is almost all prototype and then asset generation. We want to make it look good. We're planning stuff out, that kind of stuff. So that's really not how it started.

IGN: So, you basically built from scratch again? Did you take assets from the original Mass Effect 3?

Mgamerz: Oh yeah, the whole thing ports from it. It's not a one-to-one port. We're not just taking Mass Effect 3 multiplayer and dumping it into Legendary Edition and then, 'Hey guys, check out it's multiplayer, [as] you remember it.' Where we took a lot of extra steps, the lighting actually gets re-baked in Unreal Engine 4's light solver.

Essentially what that means is, imagine you have a light bulb in a room and if you wanted to project what the lights would look like, a light beam's going to hit your microphone and it's going to cast a shadow.

And then that light bounces off for you, goes into your closet and it bounces off and illuminates the closet a little bit from the inside. Unreal Engine 3 had a solver and that's how all of the lighting for all the Unreal Engine 3 games worked. But in Unreal Engine 4, they added like, 'Oh, we can do additional light bounces or we found a better statistical way to do light bounces.' And so you get crisper shadow edges or the more soft, like a grate covering on some maps. The light bounces through the grate, and unless you have super high resolution textures, it looks terrible. Mass Effect 3 is full of terrible light maps. If you look at them, you're like, 'Wow, it's just a big stair step of shadows and it looks bad.' And so we spent a lot of time upgrading that kind of stuff.

I modded Mass Effect 3 multiplayer for eight years before Legendary Edition came out, and there's a bunch of stuff I was like, 'Wow, I didn't even realize three of the character classes don't even use the highest-quality mesh.' So it's like BioWare made the Geth Infiltrator, and they made it at a high quality where it has all the polygons and triangles. And then as you get further away from the camera, it gets less triangles, because you can't see as much detail. But BioWare was just like, 'We're just not going to use the highest quality one. We'll ship it in the game, but you'll never see it.' And so it's like, 'Oh, well, we can just turn those on and it's an immediate quality upgrade.'

IGN: Was quality a big reason why you took on this massive undertaking to bring ME3 multiplayer to Legendary Edition? Because if I understand correctly, the servers for the original ME3 multiplayer are still working, for now at least.

Mgamerz: By the time we publish this, I don't know, man. N7HQ's gone, so I wouldn't be surprised if it disappears before.

Actually, the whole reason this project started, I was getting to the end of LE2 Randomizer and I was like, 'Man, I love Mass Effect 3 multiplayer.' I modded tons of stuff into it, and it was really fun.

I went back and I was like, 'I want to make a new one. I want to make a new mod.' I went back to it and I was like, 'These tools,' and I'm totally throwing myself under the bus, 'These tools suck. There's no debug tools. Everything is so immature compared to what we have in Legendary Edition, thanks to what BioWare changed for us.' And so I was like, 'Man, I'd rather just port multiplayer than have to deal with this awful development environment.'

And then I was like, 'Okay, well, I've modeled this forever.' I know where all of the pain points are in extending this because I made a new map pack, I made a new enemy pack that adds a new faction. So I'm like, 'I know where all the landmines were, because I had to pioneer it.' And I'm like, 'What if we rebuilt multiplayer and accounted for those landmines so if someone else wants to do it, they don't have to go through the same landmines, or they're at least aware that they're there?' So there's a bunch of considerations for extensibility.

As a user, if you just go in and you just play Standard, you might not notice the changes, but the next dev who wants to add a new faction, it'll be like, 'Wow, I don't have to deal with all these stupid problems that I would've had in the original game.' And so a lot of stuff like that that people won't appreciate, but will make a difference in the long run.

IGN: And it'll probably mean more mods end up coming out for it, as well. So, I'm sure you had a certain amount of people that you expected to play this once you launched it. How much did BioWare's closure change your expectations for your launch date?

Mgamerz: We were already targeting N7 Day. It was probably about in early August, late July. We were getting to a point where it was like, okay, this is fully playable. It doesn't crash. The shaders look right. It's like, this is something we could probably ship by N7 Day. I was more like, We should probably ship this in January.

But then I was like, it's N7 Day . I hate doing the N7 Day crunch, but I always do it, because I secretly feel like I'm a masochist and I kind of enjoy it. There's a satisfaction of essentially killing yourself to get the thing out the door and then being like, oh, it's finally done.

I am a hundred percent ready as of this interview to ship this thing. There's so much stress going on around this release that's killing me. But Bioware's closure, honestly, didn't really factor into it [the release date] at all.

IGN: Do you think you're going to get more people checking it out though?

Mgamerz: Oh yeah, because there's tons of attention on Mass Effect right now, so I'm sure there's going to be a lot more, which is adding to the stress. I've done launches like this for years, and I know on the first day, stuff's going to be broken. I mean, I've been developing software, the mod manager and stuff, and you launch a new feature and some user clicks a button you didn't think they'd click at the exact frame of the installer or whatever, and the whole thing dies. So I'm expecting the first day to just be kind of a train wreck, which sucks, but it's just how it is. It'll get better over time.

IGN: Do you expect that EA is going to pull access to some of the tools that are necessary for modding the game?

Mgamerz: I don't think so. We had an NDA with BioWare back in 2021. It's expired by now, but they had my dev team, not the current dev team — there's a couple more members now, but more core members back then — they had us all under NDA before Legendary Edition launched, and we provided some input to help modding.

So they clearly were interested in having modders to some degree as part of it. I don't know if new EA ownership shares that same view, so it's a little concerning, but I mean, our game requires you own Mass Effect Legendary Edition. This was never going to be like DotA where, "Hey, we split the game off and you get to go do whatever." The goal has always been, "You own Mass Effect Legendary Edition. We're going to source assets from it during the install."

Our game is technically self-contained, so it's not like a mod into Mass Effect 3. It generates a new copy of essentially Mass Effect 3, we call it LMP, and it's fully standalone. So all of your existing mods, they actually don't work with the new install by design because we don't want people immediately installing and immediately breaking everything.

It's one of those landmines that working on the old stuff, I know for a fact doing that will break multiplayer for a lot of people. So I'd rather be more restrictive at launch and then relax it as we figure it out versus, "Hey guys, here's all this stuff. You install a bunch of mods and then it just doesn't work on day one." And you're like, "Well, I'm never going to come back to this again."

IGN: Yeah. Are you hoping to support this project long term, then?

Mgamerz: Yes. Yes. Multiplayer is my jam, dude. I racked up thousands of hours, probably at least a thousand hours in the first year before Origin even tracked how long you played the game. And then I have another 2,800 hours on top of that, and most of it was modding multiplayer. And then I don't even know how much I have in Legendary Edition. I don't really play Legendary Edition. I never really played the original games, either. It was just always multiplayer. Everyone that's ever interviewed me is like, "You must love the story." And I'm like, "I've played the trilogy, the actual trilogy played through maybe twice since 2012."

IGN: So if you weren't really into the story of Mass Effect, how did you get into the multiplayer?

Mgamerz: Oh, well, I played Mass Effect 1 shortly before Mass Effect 3 came out because [of] the ads. It was actually on GameSpot. It was just littered with ads. You couldn't do anything on the page without there being a Mass Effect 3 ad. And I was like, "Oh, that looks kind of cool." And so I played Mass Effect 1. I used some texture mods and made it look better. I'm like, "Oh, this is kind of a nice game. I'm enjoying this."

And then Mass Effect 2 was pretty good. Then I got to Mass Effect 3, played about halfway through it, and then I was like, "Ah, maybe I'll try multiplayer." And then it was fun. I had a good time.

And this is where my modding career on this game started. I was playing, it was on Firebase White, and every enemy was a husk, and there were 30 of them, and my poor laptop was dying.

There were 30, but my computer was like, "Kill me, just end me right now." I remember asking on voice chat in the game, I was like, "Is anyone else's game freaking out? Why is it all husks?" And some other person was like, "I don't know, man, it must be some sort of glitch." And I was like, "Huh, weird glitch." And obviously now I know that the person was modding the game, but I had so much fun. I was like, "Man, how do I do that?" And then I learned how to do it and made my little mod manager, and then I just kept getting more and more ambitious until here we are porting multiplayer.

IGN: How did you get your start in modding? Was it with Mass Effect 1? Those texture mods?

Mgamerz: No. My technical first part of modding was SimCity 4 when I made the world's worst 3D model of a library. I think it's still on Simtropolis. I won't tell you my original username, but it was essentially just a donut and a block underneath it, and everyone roasted me for it because it was so trash. I was like 13 or something. I was super young. I didn't know what I was doing.

But then my real modding started. I got into GameMaker, which is a game development app. It was really great for learning how to program without having to learn how to program. It taught you concepts like a random chance is a dice roll. That's something everyone could understand. So it was a visual language, and I made a couple of small games. They were really fun. I really enjoyed it.

And then I found a decompiler for something called Ninja Fight Screensaver, and it's just two boxes with little limbs attached. It's just a physics simulation and it just moves them back and forth. And then the physics will cause the arm to swing, and they would calculate damage based on the velocity, and there'd be some stupid blood particle effects. It looked terrible, but I was like, "Man, I'd love to make my own level in this game." So I found a decompiler for a GameMaker build, decompiled the game, and found tons of unused levels and stuff. I was like, "Whoa, this is awesome. There's a truck in this," which was never in the released version of the game, but it's like, "Oh my God, they made a truck." I was like, "That's awesome."

And then I actually got into Mega Man Battle Network modding back in the old days. I remember doing online net battles before the Legacy Collection, before CapCom re-released it. And I was like, "Man, I remember doing that back in the day playing other players like 2006 or something." And that was all assembly modding. You have to learn how to read pretty much machine code. Really difficult, but really fun. Very dedicated little community. I took a break from modding for a couple of years, and then Mass Effect 3.

IGN: How do you feel about the pervasiveness of cloud-based AI decompilation ports and the mashup mods?

Mgamerz: Boy, it's a mix. So for the first two years of this project, we didn't even use AI at all. If you could use it, which I never did, it probably wasn't up to par to get any of the stuff done that we would really need it to do. There's been some mods recently released in this scene, and I'm not going to mention any names. I'm not targeting any specific ones.

In the modding community, you have an ecosystem. For example, I have my mod manager, you deploy mods through the mod manager, it runs a bunch of checks on the mods to make sure you're not going to ship something that's just going to break someone's game immediately. And there's certain knowledge, like you don't put stuff in startup files because it wastes tons of memory. If you stuff everything in there, you boot the game, oh, now the game takes an extra gigabyte of memory for your single mod to work because you didn't want to do it the proper way.

So there's an ecosystem of knowledge that when you start modding, you have to integrate yourself into so you can play nice with everyone's stuff. Is it as convenient as typing a prompt into Claude, "Hey, make me this mod?" Of course not. For our AI usage, and in relation to your question, there's a difference between what I call vibe coding, where you just kind of prompt it until you get what you want, and having expertise in understanding what it's actually writing and you're reviewing it, that's more like AI assisted. For decompilation specifically, we've used Claude for some of it, but a majority of our decomp was already done before AI tools were even available.

I can tell you from just seeing what it can do, it's insane how good it is. The problem is when you make it so... This will sound like gatekeeping, and it kind of is. I'm just being honest with you, it's kind of gatekeeping. The difficulty of making mods and getting into it filtered out a lot of low-quality stuff. You see this on stuff like the Switch eShop. It's full of slop, because there's no quality control, and you can just ship whatever, and then users have to dredge through all sorts of stuff like that.

There's a balance. I want to make my tools easy for people to use. I don’t want it to be like, you have to be the most masochistic person to get into modding, but I also don't want it to be like you type a prompt into Claude and you can just ship something that doesn't have any awareness of [whether] it's going to break everything else.

We've seen mods where the description and the images of the mod are not even human-written. The directions are straight up wrong. The images don't even show the content. For me personally, it's really killing it. I want there to be... I'm not saying the people that do this aren't passionate, but they don't give a damn about how it affects anyone else, because when their stuff doesn't work and it breaks, they're not going to be the ones that are around here supporting and trying to figure out why it doesn't work. It's going to be everyone else that's been here for a while that wants to fix it.

IGN: What do you think the pathway for people now who are trying to get into modding, but the only thing they're exposed to is the AI tools?

Mgamerz: I've actually thought about this a lot in the last two or three weeks. Someone released a... I don't want to say... To me, it feels like it's vibe-coded. The developer says it's not, but I feel like the difference is I have a lot more understanding of the game than the person that worked on that. So it's however you want to interpret it. I don't know.

Getting into [modding]? I feel like modding is kind of dying. If you come in and you're like, "I want to just do this, no AI. I just want to cut my teeth, find the boundaries, break over them, have a difficult, challenging task," you pretty much have to work in secret now, because if you essentially have an idea and someone else is like, "Wow, that's a cool idea." And you're like, "Well, it's going to take me six months." And they're like, "I don't want to wait six months." They can spend 20 bucks and pump this thing out in a day or two, and it'll probably work, but the user will have no understanding of how.

The best way I can describe this is: When I moved into my house a couple years ago, I did my own roof and it sucked, and it saved me money, but it was ridiculously hard work. But at the end of the day, when I'm sitting in my house and it's raining, I'm freaking out, "Is it working? Is the roof working here?" But the difference is I can believe in the craftsmanship of my work. I can know that I did it right, hopefully, versus me just paying someone else and hoping it works.

I don't get any satisfaction that I paid somebody 6,000, 10,000 bucks to do my roof. I can take satisfaction and pride that I broke my back, got sunburns, and was up there doing the hard labor. And I feel like there's value in that that is completely being eroded by the fact that you can just prompt something to get you there.

But I do understand the flip side that, if you don't have the technical skills to do it and there's realistically no chance you'll get there, it isn't fair to say, "Well, you shouldn't be able to make mods. You shouldn't be able to, 'Oh, I want that cool thing to be there.'" It's like an impossible question to answer. If you don't release the stuff that you make, I don't see any problem. You made something cool for yourself, but once you hand this product over to somebody else, share it with the world, suddenly it can become everybody's problem. And from my experience, everyone that vibe codes stuff, two weeks later, they're gone. They're not supporting it. So the people that stick around have to fix and deal with all of it.

IGN: Going back to ME3 Multiplayer, once it ships, what's next? I know that you're using it as a way to basically port the Mass Effect 3 modding scene into the Legendary Edition. Are you going to work on more Mass Effect 3 mods, or do you have your eyes on something else?

Mgamerz: Boy, I've been like, "Oh man, I need to find another game to mod for years." And then I always come back to this one, because it's just my bread and butter. I'm comfortable. I know what I'm doing. There's always some new technical challenge.

Honestly, the only projects I foresee myself doing from now on till the end of when I'm just done modding this game, I wanted to do my LE1 randomizer and my LE3 randomizer that I teased four years ago, and then just never had the willpower to finish. Because I've watched streamers play my randomizers and they're always dying laughing, the chat's having a great time. And I just watch that and I'm like, "Man, I love seeing people have tons of stupid fun with my mods."

Even if only 50 people play it, if someone had an absolutely hilarious [time], like when I was watching Criken, I was like, "It fills me with so much joy to see that." And then the other mod, obviously, I have my Map Pack, Redemption. Rejection is the enemy faction. I want to bring those up to the standard of my work these days now that our tools are modern. I really like gameplay modding. Some of our modders are like, "I have outfits, I have some story stuff," and I'm like, "I just want to have a different gameplay experience."

One of the big things I remember that ties directly into that statement, I was modding Mass Effect 3 before the Earth DLC came out in 2012. I had been modding wave lists, so the enemy factions changed, and I was editing the stats. I remember when they announced Platinum, like, "Oh, we have this new harder faction." And I'm like, "Oh, that's cool." And then it came out and I'm like, "It's just a bunch of enemies with more health and damage, and it's just like a stat boost." I was upping enemy counts. It'd be the same difficulty as a lower one, but there'd be more enemies, so you had to be more aware of what was going on.

I was like, "Man, this thing sucks." I'm like, "I'd like mine way better." And so I've always been about, “Let's make the gameplay more dynamic and different. Let's give somebody something different to play.”

IGN: So have you seen the stuff that has come out about Mass Effect Universe since BioWare’s closure?

Mgamerz: Oh, yeah. In fact, I actually have the game up on my other monitor. We actually have, we're putting new banners in and we have a bunch of banners from the trailer because I'm like, "Well, this is dead." So we're taking some content from that, that trailer, the banners. We're adding a bunch of those, but we're putting a bunch of ones in from MEU, I guess is the short name. At least that's what I call it.

It's like a bar crawler, and it's a picture of the bar scene. It's just cosmetics. I always loved earning banners and having a little thing I can show [off], so adding more of that. That's one way we're incorporating some of that. I didn't actually watch [the trailer] until two or three days after it came out, and I thought it looked pretty cool. I was glad that at least if what the trailer was showing was where the game was actually going to end up going, I thought an investigative find... ME1 was like, "Find the conduit." This is kind of like, “Find Shepard,” orsomething. I don't know. It seemed like they were doing more of an investigative kind of thing, and I thought that was kind of cool.

IGN: And also from the leaks, it sounded like the gameplay was going to be a lot more action focused. Would you have been interested in a potential MEU multiplayer?

Mgamerz: Yeah, I would love to have seen newer multiplayer. Andromeda's multiplayer was not my cup of tea. I did not like it, so I didn't really play it.

But if it was more... I mean, it doesn't have to be Mass Effect 3 multiplayer, but I prefer more on-ground stuff, because it provides a lot more limited movement patterns for enemies that are more realistic to what me, as a human, can understand, than when enemies can come out of literally any piece of geometry.

It's like, I have expectations of what a person can do. I'm in a game where I can see what the people are running around doing. I'm not thinking about them flying up in the air and stuff and that kind of stuff, but it can work either way. It just needed to be executed better.

IGN: What do you think of Exodus and The Expanse: Osiris Reborn?

Mgamerz: I honestly have not looked at them at all. I have heard that some ex-BioWare devs or Mass Effect devs are on them, but that's literally all I know about it. I watched the Expanse show. I don't know if I watched all of the seasons. I thought it was great, but I literally have been so dead laser focused on this the last couple of months that I haven't really done anything else. I haven't watched any TV shows or anything. I haven't played any other games.

Mgamerz: Yeah, that's pretty regular. I haven't done one in two years, but as you get close to the end, it's like, man, I'm working 16 hours a day trying to get this thing done.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: 'I Feel Like Modding is Kind Of Dying' – Mass Effect 3 Multiplayer Modder on AI's Impact on the Scene
articles.summary: Over the past few months, there's been a sort of explosion of AI in the modding scene. Whether it's mashup mods on Twitter or full decompilation done by Claude, AI is everywhere in the mod community, and it may just be killing the hobby.
articles.body:
Over the past few months, there's been an explosion of AI in the modding scene. Whether it's mashup mods on Twitter or full decompilation done by Claude , AI is everywhere in the mod community, and it could be killing the hobby.

I got a chance to sit down with ME3Tweaks' Mgamerz to talk about his new Mass Effect Legendary Edition ME3 Multiplayer mod, where I asked him about how AI has affected the modding community. While he admits that Claude is very effective at modding games, it's causing an avalanche of low-effort content that's hard to sift through. And, while there has always been a range of quality for mods, the inherent difficulty of getting into a game's files and changing things was a natural filter that's slowly eroding.

Mgamerz told me, "The difficulty of making mods and getting into it filtered out a lot of low-quality stuff. You see this on stuff like the Switch eShop, I've heard. It's full of slop, because there's no quality control and you can just ship whatever, and then users have to dredge through all sorts of stuff like that."

Although typing in a prompt to mod your own copy of a game is one thing, the problems start to appear once you start distributing it on platforms like Nexus Mods, where you have to be mindful about how your mod will interact with other add-ons, otherwise you're likely to just break peoples' games.

Mgamerz laid out that process, telling me, "In the modding community, you have an ecosystem. For example, I have my mod manager, you deploy mods through the mod manager, it runs a bunch of checks on the mods to make sure you're not going to ship something that's just going to break someone's game immediately."

These AI mods can do more than just break other people's mods too — they can also make your game much harder to run if they aren't optimized properly. For example, Mgamerz says, "There's certain knowledge, like you don't put stuff in startup files because it wastes tons of memory. If you stuff everything in there, you boot the game, oh, now the game takes an extra gigabyte of memory for your single mod to work, because you didn't want to do it the proper way."

It's hard to argue with the fact that these AI tools are introducing a whole new generation of gamers to modding, but it's doing so without making them go through the effort of figuring out how to make things effectively. We've already seen major modding communities pull their sites down because of this outbreak of AI modding tools that can take months of someone's hard work and spin it around into a 'working' mod after a couple of Claude prompts. And that might end up becoming the default for people who learn how to code exclusively through AI tools.

When I asked Mgamerz what the pathway for people who want to get into modding these days is, his answer was grim. He told me, "Getting into [modding]? I feel like modding is kind of dying. If you come in and you're like, 'I want to just do this, no AI. I just want to cut my teeth, find the boundaries, break over them, have a difficult, challenging task,' you pretty much have to work in secret now."

"Because if you essentially have an idea and someone else is like, 'Wow, that's a cool idea.' And you're like, 'Well, it's going to take me six months.' And they're like, 'I don't want to wait six months.' They can spend 20 bucks and pump this thing out in a day or two, and it'll probably work, but the user will have no understanding of how."

11 Mass Effect Characters and Moments the TV Show Needs to Be a Hit

Mgamerz understands, though, that the prevalence of these AI tools is getting a lot of people interested in modding their favorite games, and that's not a bad thing. He told me, "If you don't release the stuff that you make, I don't see any problem. You made something cool for yourself."

Instead, the problem is that, if you install it without considering how it'll interact with other software, it can really bungle other peoples' projects. "Once you hand this product over to somebody else, share it with the world, suddenly it can become everybody's problem. And from my experience, everyone that vibe codes stuff, two weeks later, they're gone. They're not supporting it. So the people that stick around have to fix and deal with all of it."

Ever since Claude Opus 5.5 released back in September, it feels like the modding scene has been going through a rollercoaster, and it's impossible to know where exactly it's going to land. Whether the world of Nexus Mods and publicly available GitHub forks is going to start to die down like Mgamerz thinks it will is anyone's guess. But one thing's for sure: Once The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel drops, modding is going to be a completely different animal than the Skyrim days, if Bethesda's next game is even moddable at all.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Mass Effect Cast Celebrates N7 Day With Video Asking Fans to Help Save the Franchise
articles.summary: Without BioWare, N7 Day is quieter this year, but that didn't stop the Normandy cast and crew from teaming up for a video message asking fans to help save Mass Effect.
articles.body:
Without BioWare, N7 Day is quieter this year, but that didn't stop the Normandy cast and crew from teaming up for a video message asking fans to help save Mass Effect.

EA shuttered BioWare , canceled Mass Effect 5 , and put the gaming side of the franchise on an indefinite hold just weeks before the series' annual November 7 holiday, leaving players just as hurt as they were confused. There's not really any official festivities to enjoy this year, but the developers and actors behind the stories and characters fans love still made sure to get together for a special video message.

Organized by the unofficial group known as We are Mass Effect, the two-minute video message features appearances from composer Sam Hulick, Jennifer Hale (Commander Shepard/FemShep), Ash Sroka (Tali'Zorah), Keythe Farley (Thane), Kimberly Brooks (Ashley), Mark Meer (Commander Shepard/MaleShep), Steve Blum (Urdnot Grunt), Brandon Keener (Garrus), and many more. One by one, they each call to "Save Mass Effect" in the wake of BioWare's closure, marking what is only the latest shot to garner attention and, hopefully, give the franchise a shot in the arm.

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect. — We are Mass Effect - #SaveMassEffect (@WeAreMassEffect) November 7, 2026

Today is a very special day for Mass Effect fans. We've worked incredibly hard to bring together most of the original Mass Effect trilogy's voice cast to share a very important message with you. We need to #SaveMassEffect.

"It started feeling like Shepard recruiting the squad in Mass Effect 2!" We are Mass Effect's Mer told IGN when describing the process to make the video. "We were bringing people on board one by one, and Mark was a huge help in making that happen! It almost felt like we were gathering War Assets. And the most surprising thing is that with every video we received, the actors would thank us.

"We'd get messages saying, 'Thank you for doing this,' or 'Thank you for your work.' We were the ones who felt incredibly grateful to them for taking the time to participate, but they kept turning around and thanking us. That really touched me. Everyone involved, from the people who made these games to the people who brought their characters to life, cares deeply about this universe."

We are Mass Effect and other Mass Effect fans have been busy the last few weeks. After footage and details for the canceled Mass Effect: Universe appeared online just days after EA brought the franchise to a halt, a petition has launched and gained more than 310,000 signatures . A Canadian politician also started a government petition to save BioWare just last week.

As some have called to boycott EA , others have taken their fight straight to the publisher's front door . We are Mass Effect has been a big part of that initiative, with its first and most notable move arriving when it launched a #SaveMassEffect billboard in Times Square . Yesterday, the group drove a mobile billboard around EA headquarters in Redwood City, California . More billboards are live today, including one posted up around the former BioWare offices in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, with another set to appear around The Game Awards next month. Former project director and executive producer Michael Gamble also sent a message to fans for N7 Day.

🚨 WE ARE TAKING OVER TEXAS A member of our community, AngryBaby, has put up #SaveMassEffect billboards in the Frisco and Dallas areas of North Texas. It's incredible to see fans taking the initiative and spreading the movement on their own. HOLD THE LINE 🫡 — We are Mass Effect - #SaveMassEffect (@WeAreMassEffect) November 6, 2026

"We're still holding on to that hope and fighting for the future of Mass Effect, BioWare, and the people who have dedicated so much of themselves to bringing this universe to life," Mer added. "N7 Day is a reminder of what these games mean to all of us, but also of the people behind them. The impact they've had on this community will never been forgotten, and we will continue celebrating it for as long as we can."

Meanwhile, as the Mass Effect cast and fans on the ground do their best to celebrate N7 Day, other developers have chimed in to share their love for the series on its saddest holiday so far. Owlcat Games, the team behind the upcoming Mass Effect-inspired RPG The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, shared a video celebrating what BioWare and its work over the decades means to them.

"Everybody in Owlcat dreamt about playing Mass Effect 5," studio creative director Alexander Mishulin said. "It's very, very selfish, but we wanted to experience the next chapter in those adventures. Our hearts and minds are with [BioWare], and we really hope they find themselves a new home, different studios that will allow them to make even more worlds, even more experiences, more adventures that we will be amazed at. That will be new beacons for new generations of game developers.

"It will be not Mass Effect, but it will be something else, and something beautiful."

articles.title: Sony Announces Indefinite Delay for PlayStation's Pulse Elevate Wireless Speakers Days Before Launch
articles.summary: Sony has announced an indefinite delay for PlayStation's Pulse Elevate wireless speakers just days before their global launch.
articles.body:
Sony has announced an indefinite delay for PlayStation's Pulse Elevate wireless speakers just days before their global launch.

The tech company announced the last-minute schedule change in a November 6, 2026, update to an existing PlayStation.Blog post . The message cites a recently identified "production issue" that must be attended to, with no new release date shared.

"As part of our ongoing quality testing of Pulse Elevate speakers, we have identified a production issue with the product and have made the decision to delay the launch," Sony's announcement said. "The additional time will allow us to ensure the product will deliver the experience we intended for our players. We apologize for the delay and appreciate your patience and understanding. We look forward to bringing Pulse Elevate to players soon."

PlayStation Pulse Elevate Wireless Speakers

Scroll the tiniest bit further down, and you'll see that Sony had set the Pulse Elevate speakers to launch globally November 12 – just six days out from when the delay update was published. Whatever problem its team encountered must have been pretty significant, but without a new release date or additional information, it's unclear if we'll learn what happened.

Sony announced its new PlayStation-branded, $219.99 speakers in September of last year as the latest entry in its collection of Pulse audio accessories, which includes earbuds and headphones. They were said to be available in both Midnight Black and White, with both boasting a built-in microphone with "AI-enhanced noise rejection." The speakers are also able to be paired with PlayStation 5, PC, Mac, and even PlayStation Portal devices.

"Pulse Elevate builds upon the immersive next-level gaming audio experience we introduced to players with Pulse Elite wireless headset and Pulse Explore wireless earbuds, combining powerful technologies like planar magnetic drivers and PlayStation Link into new form factors for players to experience with their favorite games," Sony said at the time of the announcement.

How many units were manufactured ahead of the delay, or how the new issue may impact these existing speakers, was not made immediately clear. IGN took a closer look at all of the new PlayStation hardware, Pulse Elevate wireless speakers included, back in June. We came away looking forward to how the tech might work in practice, calling its noise rejection system "seriously impressive stuff."

“Hearts and Noses” is one of the Special Gathering Quests for Wish me mell’s Birthday on September 20 in Hello Kitty Island Adventure . By completing this quest, you can celebrate your favorite gardener’s birthday and be rewarded with a Wish me mell Party Favor and Wish me mell’s Birthday Balloons Crafting Plans.

Wish me mell’s Birthday Quest will be available on September 18th and time out a few days after her birthday on September 24 . If you’ve already completed this quest, then “Hearts and Noses” will not appear again, but you can still collect Wish me mell Decorating Kits around this time.

Wish me mell’s Decorating Kits can occasionally be found when picking up items around Merry Meadows , such as Pollen Puff and Worm Tails. You can use these Decorating Kits to make a special birthday cake just for Wish me mell!

To begin the quest, first talk to Wish me mell in Merry Meadows. She shares that she’ll be having a birthday party in Merry Meadows and is excited to get started, only.. she’s got a bit of a tickle in her nose. Wish me mell’s allergies are acting up thanks to the abundance of flowers throughout Friendship Island, and although she says she doesn’t need help, her sneezes tell a different story.

Help Wish me mell out with her tasks so she can enjoy her birthday in peace. First, she’ll need a couple of flowers that aren’t native to Merry Meadows. If you have them, be sure to gift Wish me mell:

Check in on With me mell again. Her allergies are really giving her a hard time, so you suggest taking the last leg of her list of things to do to give her some much-needed rest. First, Wish me mell needs a couple of Strawberry Shortcakes picked up from Hello Kitty’s Cafe, some Rubber and Thread to be delivered to My Melody , and a couple of Gift Boxes crafted for her guests that will arrive.

Head to Hello Kitty’s Cafe first to check on the order. She’s been a bit busy, so she asks if you can put your baking skills to the test by helping her out to make some cakes for Wish me mell. For Wish me mell’s order, you’ll need to make 5x Strawberry Shortcakes .

Strawberry Shortcakes Recipe: 1x Flour (My Melody’s Daily Gift) and 1x Strawberry ( Pochacco’s Daily Gift)

With that complete, talk to Hello Kitty to complete the task. Head over to My Melody next. It seems like she was tasked with crafting something for Wish me mell’s birthday, but she’ll need a couple of items to get started. Gift My Melody:

5x Thread ( Tuxedosam’s Daily Gift. Can also be found outside the Creation Station )

With that task out of the way, all that’s left are the Gift Boxes. Head to Chococat’s Tent to use his Crafting Table. Be sure to inform Chococat that it’s Wish me mell’s birthday today, and there’ll be a party in Merry Meadows so that he doesn’t miss it. Use Chococat’s Crafting Table to craft 5x Gift Boxes .

Gift Box Recipe: 1x Box Clam ( Rainbow Reef ) and 1x Starfish (Rainbow Reef)

With Wish me mell’s list complete, head back to Merry Meadows to let her know her tasks are all done! She’s sad that she wasn’t able to do all she wanted for her birthday and completely forgot she asked you for help! Gift Wish me mell the Strawberry Shortcakes and the Gift Boxes that you helped to make.

Head to the party with Wish me mell so that you can celebrate your favorite gardener. Although she wasn’t able to make everyone a garland, her friends are much happier to celebrate her instead. Although she couldn’t finish the Flower Crowns in time, she does have a Wish me mell Party Favor and Wish me mell Birthday Balloons Crafting Plans for you as the quest comes to an end.

articles.title: Shadow Temple Dungeon Walkthrough - The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Guide - IGN
articles.summary: Welcome to IGN's Guide to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake. After 28 years, Ocarina of Time has been fully remade, and while much of it remains
articles.body:
Welcome to IGN's Guide to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake. After 28 years, Ocarina of Time has been fully remade, and while much of it remains the same, there's plenty of new differences to be found while exploring Hyrule. The attack on Kakariko Village may have been thwarted, but a sinister presence still lurks in the Shadow Temple beyond the Graveyard. Link will need to uses his new Lenses of Truth to reveal the evil and assist the Shadow Sage in sealing the darkness.

Now that you've obtained the Lenses of Truth from Beneath the Well in the past, Link can now return to Kakariko Village as an adult, using the Nocturne of Shadow that Sheik passed down to find the secret entrance to the Shadow Temple overlooking the Graveyard.

Entering the Shadow Temple's depths, you'll be greeted with an ominous room and a plaque decreeing "Those who lack the eyes of truth are not granted the way forward". Equip your Lenses of Truth, and you'll see what they mean.

A large circle of unlit braziers line the center of the room, invisible to the naked eye. This is the secret mechanism preventing access to the temple, but now that you know what's hidden, you can take the steps to opening the sealed door. Use Din's Fire while standing in the middle of the room to light all of the braziers at once, and the way forward will be open to you.

Heading through into the corridor beyond, be ready for an ambush by Flying Pots, and stand your ground with shield raised to let them crash harmlessly into pieces. Turning the corner, there's a large gap you'll need to use your Longshot to cross to the far side. Another plaque waits here in front of a wall, again warning you "To the fool who defies the darkness, know that without the eyes of truth, there is no path". You can consider that an extra warning if you were able to make it through the first area by a "lucky guess"...

Equipping the Lens of Truth at this seemingly dead end, you'll find its not an end at all, and you can simply walk through the creepy face into the room beyond.

More walls lined with creepy faces can be found here, along with a large imposing deathbird statue bearing a handhold as well as a plaque that reads "The tip of my beak seeks the skull of truth. Should it find falsehood, darkness shall fall". Seems ominous!

What this means is that of the small columns around the statue lined with skulls, only one is the "skull of truth". Put on your Lenses of Truth and you'll see what they mean - all but one will disappear! Pull the bird statue around so that the beak faces the northwest, and the door to the east will open.

There's another plaque along the floor over by a large pit at the end of the room where the door you opened is out of reach, reading "The valley of dead can only be crossed with footsteps as light as a feather". This means the way forward is closed to you until you can find a new item to help you traverse gaps like this.

For now, turn back to where the "skull of truth" was and you can find that there's a hidden doorway behind it along the northwest wall. Head through to find an ominous skull again warning you that you're really going to need to see the truth.

Beyond, you'll find a masuoleum like area lined with skulls, with another hidden doorway under a black skull to the north that your Lenses will reveal.

Head through the hidden door, and you'll enter a room that will seal behind you, leaving you to battle a Redead and several Keese. Remember to use your Sun's Song if you need to stun the foe, otherwise keep strafing behind the Redead to slash at its back so it can't hit you with its paralzying beam. Defeating the room will reveal a large Treasure Chest holding a Dungeon Map!

The map will also help reveal the location of some hidden passageways you may have easily missed unless you were looking around carefully with the Lenses of Truth. One such room appears to be an identical masolueum square room west of the first one, and you can find a hidden opening along the western wall.

Head through this next small room and be ready to deal with more Flying Pots, as well as a Wallmaster that may try to yank you from above. Dodge back when the shadow grows and the spotlight turns to red to dodge and then slash it before it can escape.

There's another hidden entrance leading out of this room that your map can clue you in on, in the northwest corner of the room heading west. This leads to a long hallway that will try and jumpscare you when the floor gives out, but you can climb up the other side using the mesh wall.

In the room beyond, you'll face off against an old foe: Deadhand has returned. He's just as cagey has he was seven years ago, meaning he won't show his face until he thinks you're trapped. With that in mind, allow yourself to be grabbed by one of the hands so that he appears and starts to lumber forward, and then break free and start slashing at him before he can retreat.

Make sure not to charge in recklessly once you break free, as you can easily be grabbed by other hands and leave yourself open to getting chomped.

Thankfully, your adult weapons deal a whole lot more damage than your Kokiri Sword, so it won't take a whole lot of punishment to bring down Deadhand for good. As he falls, a large Treasure Chest will appear holding this temple's treasure: The Hover Boots!

These boots are the polar opposite of the Iron Boots, and are mapped to down on the D-pad as well once selected. When stepping off a ledge, you'll no longer drop straight down, and instead float in the air for several moments, with the momentum of your steps carrying you across gap. The only downside is they make your movements a bit slippery -- as if you were running on ice, so it's best to unequip them when moving normally or in combat unless absolutely necessary.

Try them out by running back through the previous hallway, and the Hover Boots will send you clear across to the other side!

Return to the room with the creepy bird statue, and be sure to point its beak to the one real skull column in the northwest if you haven't already. You'll now be able to equip your Hover Boots to dash across the pit and onto the creepy tongue-platform on the far side and continue one.

The room ahead is guarded by a Beamos, and also sports a large cracked wall on the far side: two things easily solved by a well placed bomb toss! However, a locked door waits for you on the other side, and when consulting your map, you can spot rooms to the north and south.

Sure enough, your Lenses of Truth will reveal the other two walls to be fake. Take the path to the south first to enter the room below. The door will seal behind you, forcing you into another close-quarters battle -- this time with two Gibdos. These mummies are tougher variants to the ReDeads, and can prove quite tenacious. You can try using Din's Fire to burn both at the same time, just be sure you keep some distance if they try to paralyze you and then stagger quickly to latch on and sap your life!

Defeating the pair will reveal a new large Treasure Chest holding the Compass, which can further help you get your bearings in this mysterious temple.

Take the path north next, which leads to a large room with an unsettling sight: A large statue of twin robed figures slowly spin two large scythes around the room. As the statues spin, you can spot five silver Rupees that have been placed around the room, and you'll need to move quickly and carefully to gather them all.

Follow a scythe as it passes to grab the first silver Rupee, then race to the northeast side and jump up to clamber on a thin wooden barrier with the second Rupee as the scythes cleave through below you.

From here, you can leap to an alcove in the north to find a third silver Rupee. Note a strange plaque in the alcove nearby, which reads "Approach if you seek the ferry to the afterlife". Step forward and you'll fall down an invsibile hole all the way to floor B4 where you can view a large skeleton ship, but the way forward is blocked from this approach.

Back in the scythe room, dash over between the scythes to another wooden barrier, and look for the fourth silver Rupee on a high ledge with a Longshot target you can zip to while above the scythes.

Finally, time your leap down to the west alcove to grab the last silver Rupee. This opens up an area on the opposite side of the room containing the first Small Key, just be sure you make your way over to it carefully.

Open up the locked door back in the hub room where the Beamos was to head down a long twisting corridor. Move cautiously here and look for bits of drool trickling down from above to spot where several Skulltulas are waiting to drop down and ambush you.

Near the end of the hall, you'll need to drop down, and evade falling guillotines in addition to fending off a few more Skulltulas. Once at the end, take the lift down further into the basement.

You'll now find yourself in a large cavernous room, with only a few platforms over the large pit below, and bigger ledges along the south side. First, carefully time your jumps past the falling guillotines to follow the road south to the first large platform.

“Queen of Halloween” is one of the Special Gathering Quests for Kuromi’s Birthday on October 31 in Hello Kitty Island Adventure . After celebrating the Spooky Celebration Month of Mischief all month long, it’s finally time to come together and give Kuromi a real prankster’s party. By completing this quest, you can celebrate your favorite spooky witch’s birthday and be rewarded with a Kuromi Party Favor and Kuromi’s Birthday Balloons Crafting Plans .

Hangyodon at the Comedy Club ( Rainbow Reef )

Badtz-maru at the Comic Stand ( Seaside Resort )

Hello Kitty at the Hello Kitty Cafe (Seaside Resort)

Cinnamoroll on his mail run (Check the Map and look for Cinnamoroll's Icon)

articles.title: Missing Teen Saved From Alleged Kidnapper After Seeking Help in Among Us
articles.summary: A Utah teenager was rescued from an Oregon man's home after she successfully contacted help from another child in Among Us.
articles.body:
A Utah teenager was rescued from an Oregon man's home after she successfully contacted help from another child in Among Us .

Authorities saved the 17-year-old November 1, 2026, after receiving a tip relayed by a younger player she met while playing developer Innersloth's hit party mystery game, according to Newsweek . She had allegedly spent more than 500 days held captive by 39-year-old Adam Harmel after he took her across state lines and prevented her from leaving.

The Utah teen was just 15 when she was reported missing in May 2025. Harmel allegedly began contacting her through Snapchat earlier that month before offering to send her money to travel to his home in Oregon. He then made the hours-long drive to her location and lured her into his vehicle, disposing of her phone by throwing it into a river shortly after.

Investigators said Harmel forced the teenager to sleep in a bed with him in his basement, becoming increasingly violent through the 521 days she was held captive. She found her window to escape when the alleged kidnapper granted her access to a phone without cellular data.

Although unable to contact others via traditional means, the device did allow her to use a WiFi connection to play online games. Among Us, which allows players to communicate and was released for mobile devices in 2018, allowed her to get in touch with another child.

After moving the conversation to a different, undisclosed social media app, she then told the other player who she was, revealing that she was actively being held captive at Harmel's home in Oregon.

She shared concern that, after more than 500 days of searching, authorities had stopped looking for her. The other child then alerted their mother to the interaction, with the parent then reaching out to the FBI. A subsequent video call with the missing teenager saw her describe her circumstances to investigators.

She was rescued from Harmel's property later that day. Harmel has since been arrested and charged with transporting the teenager across state lines with the intent to exploit her.

articles.summary: “Bows in the Attic” is one of the Special Gathering Quests for Hello Kitty’s birthday on November 1 in Hello Kitty Island Adventure. By
articles.body:
“Bows in the Attic” is one of the Special Gathering Quests for Hello Kitty’s birthday on November 1 in Hello Kitty Island Adventure . By completing this quest, you can celebrate your favorite crafter’s birthday and be rewarded with a Hello Kitty Party Favor and Hello Kitty’s Birthday Balloons Crafting Plans .

Hello Kitty’s Birthday Quest will be available on October 30 and will time out a few days after her birthday on November 1 . If you’ve already completed this quest, then “Bows in the Attic” will not appear again, but you can still collect Hello Kitty’s Decorating Kits around this time.

Hello Kitty’s Decorating Kits can occasionally be found when picking up items around Seaside Resort , such as Sand Dollars , Rubber , and Pineapples . Use these Decorating Kits at the Oven to bake Hello Kitty a special elaborately decorated birthday cake!

To start the quest, seek out My Melody at her shop, Small Gift Big Smile . Thank goodness for your arrival; she’s been needing an accomplice! It’s Hello Kitty’s special day around the corner, and My Melody wants to surprise her with a birthday party. But it can’t be held at Seaside Resort; otherwise she’ll know what’s up. The venue will have to be located elsewhere. Scout some locations with My Melody and head to Spooky Swamp for some ideas.

Meet up with My Melody at the Haunted Mansion after traveling to Spooky Swamp. Kuromi meets you there to consider the Haunted Mansion as a possible venue. It’s got plenty of rooms and treats can be snuck in through the basement; it’s almost perfect!

Until Hello Kitty joins. She wasn’t meant to be here! Hello Kitty is in Spooky Swamp collecting Apples for baking. When asked what you’re doing there, you make up a quick excuse.

After Hello Kitty says her farewells, My Melody concludes that Spooky Swamp won’t do if Hello Kitty can find out what they are up to. Looks like you’ll need to continue searching for venues.

Following Kuromi’s suggestion, fast travel to the Dance Hall in Gemstone Mountain . It’s got plenty of room to dance and is far away from Seaside Resort. Pekkle is there already, dancing on the floor, and asks if you’re there to join.

My Melody explains her plan, and Pekkle welcomes the idea. The Dance Hall has plenty of room for decorations and dancing, plus they have tables for lots of snacks. It could just be the perfect place for Hello Kitty’s secret birthday party!

Until the birthday girl shows up once again. After another quick excuse as to why you’re suddenly at the Dance Hall, My Melody questions why Hello Kitty is in Gemstone Mountain. Once again, for her quest in baking, she has ventured to the desert for her special desserts made with Cactus Creams. Looks like this venue isn’t going to work either…

Pekkle apologizes, saying that there aren’t many secret hidey holes in the Dance Hall. This seems to give My Melody an idea, and she urges you to meet her outside her shop to finally decide on a venue.

Head back to Seaside Resort and talk to My Melody outside her shop. She has the perfect idea for a birthday party venue, and the secret lies in the attic of Small Gift Big Smile! She’s been meaning to clean up the attic, but kept putting it off. Now with Hello Kitty’s birthday around the corner, this is the perfect opportunity to spruce up the place and begin decorating!

Help My Melody clean up the attic by gathering the different boxes and planks around the room. After picking up the 4x pieces of Clutter , talk to My Melody again to find out what’s next on the list.

The place is looking better than ever, but the dust that’s stirred up is starting to aggravate everyone’s noses. My Melody suggests coming back to cleaning after you allow the dust to settle. The quest concludes, but the next step in arranging Hello Kitty’s birthday party is just around the corner.

Wait two days before checking back in with My Melody in the next quest, “A Fresh Coat of Paint.”

articles.summary: “Finding Your Groove” is one of the Special Gathering Quests for Pekkle’s Birthday on July 27 in Hello Kitty Island Adventure. By
articles.body:
“Finding Your Groove” is one of the Special Gathering Quests for Pekkle’s Birthday on July 27 in Hello Kitty Island Adventure . By completing this quest, you can celebrate your favorite dancer’s birthday and be rewarded with a Pekkle Party Favor and Pekkle’s Birthday Balloons Crafting Plans .

Pekkle’s Birthday Quest will be available for some time before and after his actual birthday, starting July 25 and ending July 31 . If you’ve already completed this quest, then “Finding Your Groove” will not appear again, but you can still find Pekkle Decorating Kits during the week of Pekkle’s Birthday.

Pekkle’s Decorating Kits can occasionally be found when picking up items around Gemstone Mountain , such as Shinies , Fizzy Ore , and Calming Crystals . You can use these Decorating Kits to make a special birthday cake just for Pekkle!

To start the quest, you’ll first need to talk to Pekkle in Gemstone Mountain. He’s happy to celebrate his birthday, but wants to try something other than dancing or a party at the Dance Hall . Pekkle wants to try out different hobbies, starting first with fishing! But first, he’ll need a good fishing spot.

While in Gemstone Town, catch any type of Fish from a body of water. You can use the small pond that’s located right there in town or use the small donut-shaped lake that’s located northeast of Gemstone Town.

Once you’ve caught a fish, talk to Pekkle again. He’s a bit… underwhelmed, but does admire your patience and persistence. This hobby is just a bit too relaxed for him; he needs something with a bit more movement. He recalls that Hello Kitty always seems busy around her cafe, so maybe you two can go check on her to see if there’s anything she might need help with today!

Head to Hello Kitty’s Cafe in Seaside Resort . She inquires about your activities for the day and Pekkle’s search for a new hobby, happy to help in any way she can. She asks that you and Pekkle commandeer the oven while she takes orders. First, she’ll need 2x Strawberry Shortcakes .

Strawberry Shortcake Recipe: 1x Flour ( My Melody’s Daily Gift) and 1x Strawberry ( Pochacco’s Daily Gift)

Once those are complete, talk to Hello Kitty for your next task. She’ll now need 3x Pineapple Stack Cakes .

Pineapple Stack Cake Recipe: 1x Flour (My Melody’s Daily Gift) and 1x Pineapple (Seaside Resort)

With those done, talk to Hello Kitty again for your new order. Now, she’ll need a whopping 4x Tofu Bread !

Tofu Bread Recipe: 1x Flour (My Melody’s Daily Gift) and 1x Tofu (Hello Kitty’s Daily Gift)

Talk to Hello Kitty once all the Tofu Bread is baked. With that, you’ve completed one order! Hello Kitty checks in on how Pekkle finds the baking experience. It was quite a doozy, and you’ve worked up quite the sweat for just one order. Pekkle finds running the cafe to be a bit of a doozy and thinks something more chill would be better suited to his style.

With two hobbies already tried and tested, Hello Kitty suggests changing up the mood instead. She advises going to Kuromi in Spooky Swamp for a change of scenery to see if you can find a perfect secondary hobby for Pekkle. Head to Spooky Swamp to talk to Kuromi for some inspiration.

A curious Pekkle asks Kuromi if spooky vibes can be a hobby, and while it’s more of a lifestyle, Kuromi suggests giving it a try by brewing a potion. Head into the Potion Hut to interact with the Cauldron and try brewing up a Deep Diving Potion .

Deep Diving Potion Recipe: 1x Glow Berries (Spooky Swamp) and 1x Sugarkelp (Keroppi’s Daily Gift)

Kuromi demands that everyone cackle upon the completion of the potion, and while Pekkle admires her commitment to the lifestyle, it may not really be his kind of vibe. He thanks Kuromi for her time, and you two reconvene back in Gemstone Mountains. Pekkle thanks you for going around the island with him and trying out new things; while he didn’t find a new hobby, he certainly loved going out and about with you! He hears something going down at the Dance Hall , and you two go to check it out.

Turns out, this is where all of Pekkle’s friends have arranged his birthday party! What a wonderful day it turned out to be! With the quest complete, you’ll be rewarded with a Pekkle Party Favor and Pekkle Birthday Balloons Crafting Plans .

articles.title: LEGO Black Friday 2026 Sales: What to Expect
articles.summary: You can expect to see plenty of deals on LEGO sets during Black Friday 2026. I've covered LEGO deals for years, and here's what I expect to see this year.
articles.body:
On nearly every IGN article about LEGO sets (and as the LEGO editor here at IGN, I post a lot of them), commenters complain that LEGO sets cost too much. That’s a fair criticism, especially because many of the most noteworthy LEGO sets are expensive .

Even the smaller sets cost more than you might expect if you don’t pay attention to the market. They’re comprised of many tiny interlocking pieces, after all. If you feel like you’re priced out of many LEGO sets you’d want to buy, Black Friday offers an excellent opportunity to buy them at some of the lowest prices of the year.

The question is, what kinds of discounts on LEGO can we expect to see this Black Friday? I’ve been covering LEGO deals for many years now, so here’s what I expect based on my experience.

Many times throughout the year, LEGO sets go on sale at various retailers. These run-of-the-mill sales generally offer discounts of 20% off. That’s the standard sale price at retailers like Amazon, Target, Best Buy, and the LEGO Store.

Therefore, a particularly good sale on LEGO sets is when you can find them for 30%, 40%, or even 50% off . These are the kinds of discounts I expect to see once the true Black Friday sales begin.

Unlike many retailers, the official LEGO Store tends to have a pretty short-lived Black Friday sale. Last year's sale started on Black Friday and ran for fours days – which means through that weekend and Cyber Monday. But the LEGO Store won't be the only retailer dropping prices on LEGO sets, so keep an eye on the Black Friday sale schedule to see when retailers like Amazon and Walmart's sales will go live.

Which brings us to the question of which sets are most likely to be discounted? Answer: the sets that are retiring soon.

LEGO releases hundreds of new sets each year ( here’s our running tally of the 2026 releases ). To make room on retailer shelves for all those new boxes, LEGO has to retires older sets at roughly the same rate. Right now, LEGO’s “retiring soon” page has over 200 sets on it. You can bet many of these will go on sale during Black Friday as retailers try to offload inventory to make way for upcoming LEGO sets .

Each year, LEGO releases a major new set on Black Friday. It’s always a statement piece, and it’s priced accordingly.

This year’s Black Friday set is LEGO Godzilla , a towering 5,363-piece set that stands over two feet tall. It features a striking gray-and-blue version of the city-wrecker that looks menacing and highly detailed. I love it. It will be available for $449.99, starting at 12:01 a.m. November 27.

If you buy it between November 27 - 30 while supplies last, you’ll also get an additional LEGO set as a free Gift With Purchase. It’s LEGO Godzilla Logo & Footprint , and it’s meant to be displayed next to the King of Monsters. It has matching colors and looks phenomenal.

Every year on the weekend before Black Friday, LEGO runs an “Insiders Weekend” promotion. This is a LEGO Store sale that’s exclusive to LEGO Insiders, a free membership that gets you access to events like this ( you can sign up here ). In addition to discounts on select sets, it also gets you things like bonus loyalty points on purchases, as well as exclusive Gifts with Purchase. You can check out last year’s promotions for an idea of what promotions we might expect to see in 2026.

Chris Reed is a senior commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's LEGO coverage and maintains the upcoming release dates articles for video games , LEGO sets , and 4K Blu-rays . You can follow him on Bluesky .

articles.title: How to Get and Use the Ship Teleportation Device - Crimson Desert Guide - IGN
articles.summary: The Ship Teleportation Device is a special blueprint that lets you fast travel directly to your ship in Crimson Desert's Charting the Unknown DLC. Without
articles.body:
The Ship Teleportation Device is a special blueprint that lets you fast travel directly to your ship in Crimson Desert 's Charting the Unknown DLC. Without it, you'll have to pay a hefty fee at a Ship Manager to to recall your vessel at one of Pywel's ports. This guide details exactly how to discover the and craft the Ship Teleportation Device.

The Ship Teleportation Device blueprint is located in a buried treasure chest on Auronui Island , the first place the Greymanes visit after obtaining a ship during the Charting the Unknown questline.

Poking around the island will lead you to a cave on the southwest coast near an Abyss Nexus fast travel point. Inside the cave, there's a Forgotten Treasure Map that reads " To the West of Auronui Island, by the coast. "

This treasure map leads you to the chest with the Ship Teleportation Device blueprint. It's on the northern coast of the western part of Auronui Island, near an Azurite deposit on the cliff and a small campsite.

The chest isn't buried particularly well, so you should be able to spot its golden sheen as you approach. Using a shovel, dig up the treasure chest and then grab the Ship Teleportation Device blueprint inside.

How to Use the Ship Teleportation Device

Once you've read and learned the Ship Teleportation Device blueprint, you can craft it at any Workstation with 15 Shiny Ore , 10 Iron Ore , and five Azurite .

Azurite can be found all over Auronui Island, and Iron Ore is incredibly common across Pywel. Shiny Ore is a new material introduced with the Charting the Unknown DLC, so you may not have any yet. You can find it in underwater deposits on the ocean floor or inside drifting boxes encountered while sailing.

With the required materials in hand, go to a Workstation and craft the device in the ship section. You can find a Workstation next to the furniture vendor at the Greymane Camp or the Timberham Sawmill in Hernand.

Once it's crafted, visit a Ship Manager at one of Pywel's ports and select Manage Ship. Then, choose your ship and select Change Equipment. This menu will allow you to equip the Ship Teleportation Device for your chosen vessel.

Once it's equipped, you can fast travel to your ship from the map as if it were an Abyss Nexus. The Ship Teleportation Device isn't universal across your fleet, so you'll need to craft more if you want to fast travel to other ships that you own.

articles.title: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
articles.summary: Nintendo has released its remake of what is considered one of the best games ever made - the BBC's Tom Gerken gives his verdict.
articles.body:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.

IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.

A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.

It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.

So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?

Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.

Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.

As I've said before , video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.

And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.

"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.

"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."

But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.

One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.

"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.

"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."

But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.

"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."

'Serious thought has gone into every decision'

I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.

Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.

"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.

"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.

"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."

Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.

"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."

And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".

"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."

Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.

Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".

He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".

I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.

As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.

At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.

Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.

I don't think the developers see it that way.

"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.

Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.

Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.

Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."

Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.

And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.

"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.
